claim: For a complex multi-part object, organize each functional group of elements (e.g. head, tank, arms -- with left/right arm as sub-collections nested inside 'arms') into its own nested collection under one main object collection, rather than leaving all parts loose in one flat collection. Each part-group's visibility can then be toggled independently.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration (1:43:04-1:43:41): 'When working with complex objects which consists out of many elements, it can be helpful to organize each group of elements into separate collections... I have a main collection... for the robot... but I also created collections for sub parts like the head, the gallon, nodes, the arms... the arms even have sub collections for the right and left arm... this can make working with a complex scene much easier since you can easily turn off different things... to only see what you need... or to try out different things without all the rest in the way.'
rejected_alternative: Keeping all of a complex object's parts (bolts, head, tank, arms, etc.) as loose objects in a single flat collection, which per the narration makes it harder to isolate or hide a specific part-group while testing or focusing on one area.
reason: This project already has a Model/low-poly collection convention (blender-modeling-technique-corrections.md #4), which splits by LOD/purpose at the top level. This tutorial's nesting is organized along a different axis -- by functional/anatomical part-group, nested arbitrarily deep -- so it looks like something that would nest inside a Model or low-poly collection rather than replace that convention, but this has not been tried on a built asset yet.

claim: Pressing M with an object selected opens a 'Move to Collection' menu that moves the selection into any existing collection, or creates-and-names a new nested collection in one step. This works even with the viewport maximized (Ctrl+Space) and the Outliner not visible.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration (1:43:48-1:44:28): '...maybe you have, with CTRL + SPACE full screen, your 3D viewport, and you don't wanna go back and show the outliner. You can use a shortcut M, to move this selected object or multiple selected objects into these existing collections. Or you can even put this into a new one, and then you can rename this and hit okay... this new collection was created inside the robot collection with the cube inside.'
rejected_alternative: Dragging the object onto the target collection row in the Outliner by hand, which requires leaving a maximized viewport to see the Outliner at all.
reason: A minor but real workflow convenience for keeping newly added objects sorted into the part-group collection scheme above without breaking a maximized viewport.

claim: To get linked-duplicate behavior (one shared source, edits propagate to every copy) across a whole multi-object group rather than a single object, create a Collection Instance of that group's collection (Shift+A > Collection Instance) instead of using Alt+D -- Alt+D linked duplication only links a single object, not a group.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration (1:44:33-1:45:43): 'duplicating something with ALT+D... creates a linked duplicate... if I change anything on one of those two objects, it will also affect the other. However, this is only possible for single objects and not for a whole group of objects unless... by creating instances of our collections... an instance of this whole collection... if I change anything over here in this collection... this will be mirrored inside the instance collection... it won't affect the size of your scene because all it does is take the information of this robot and just display it multiple times. We can still change the position of these instances and even scale and rotate them independently, but everything else is just copied from the original collection.'
rejected_alternative: Using Alt+D (linked duplicate) on each object in the group individually, or Shift+D (a fully independent copy) of the whole group -- neither keeps a multi-object group live-linked to one editable source the way a Collection Instance does.
reason: Generalizes linked-duplicate behavior from a single mesh to an arbitrary multi-object sub-assembly. Directly relevant to any future asset needing many repeated copies of a multi-part sub-object (e.g. a bolt-and-bracket assembly), since per the narration this does not add to scene data size -- instances just redisplay the source.

claim: A whole sub-collection of objects can be mirrored as one live-linked unit by creating a Collection Instance of that sub-collection (Shift+A > Collection Instance) and then applying Ctrl+M (mirror) on the desired axis to the instance object itself. Any subsequent edit to objects in the source sub-collection is then automatically mirrored onto the instance's side, without a Mirror modifier on any individual object.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration (1:46:09-1:46:44): 'let's disable the charger stuff... I wanna mirror the whole collection of this cup holder to the other side. I have this cups collection... let's select these bolts here, press M, move to collection, robot and cups... now all I need is to hit SHIFT + A collections and click on cups, and we have an instance of this sub collection. And now let's press CTRL + M for the mirroring function, in this case X axis, and mirror this to the other side. And now everything I do on the one collection here on the objects of this collection will also affect the other one.'
rejected_alternative: Manually duplicating the cup-holder's objects and mirroring the duplicate by hand (or relying on Alt+D linked duplicate per object, which per this same chapter does not work across a whole multi-object group) -- neither keeps the mirrored side live-linked to later edits on the source side.
reason: This is a genuinely different mechanism from this project's already-captured Mirror-modifier-Bisect finding (modifiers chapter): Bisect works within a single object's own mesh data via a modifier, while Mirror Collections operates across an arbitrary multi-object sub-assembly at the collection level and keeps both sides live-linked to one edit source. Worth recording as a distinct alternative for whole-object/whole-assembly symmetry, not a replacement for the per-mesh Bisect technique.

claim: A Collection Instance's origin is placed at the world/scene origin by default, regardless of where the source collection's contents actually sit -- so moving the instance moves it relative to world-center, not relative to the source geometry, which is only usable by coincidence. Fix: select an object inside the source collection, snap the 3D cursor to it (Shift+S > Cursor to Selection), then on that object's Object Properties > Collections entry choose 'Set Offset from Cursor' to reposition the whole collection's instancing origin to that point.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration (1:47:00-1:48:22): 'There's a small problem when working with instancing collections... this one here is placed into the gallon collection... if I now hit SHIFT + A collection instance and click on gallon, it will create the instance... however, if I move this to the side, you can see it will use the center of our scene here to generate the origin of this collection instance, which is, in some cases, not really usable. However we can change this by selecting one object which is inside of the original collection... use the 3D cursor... SHIFT + S cursor to selection... go to the object tab, collections... click on this dropdown and then click on set offset from cursor. Now it uses the position of this 3D cursor in context of this object, and repositions the origin of this new collection... much better to handle... But take care, as soon as you change anything on the original object here, this will certainly affect all the instances.'
rejected_alternative: Accepting the default scene-origin-based instance pivot and manually nudging each instance's position by trial and error to compensate, instead of fixing the collection's instancing origin once via the 3D-cursor offset.
reason: A concrete gotcha for the Collection Instance and Mirror Collections techniques above: any object added to a source sub-collection away from world origin will instance with an unusable default pivot unless this offset step is done once on that collection.

claim: Objects can be parented directly in the Outliner without Ctrl+P: hold Shift, select the child object's row, and drag it onto the intended parent object's row. To remove that parenting, hold Shift, select the child's row, and drag it out onto a collection row instead -- the Outliner shows a 'drop to clear parent' cue.
supporting_evidence: Per the narration (1:48:27-1:49:20): 'Parenting objects onto each other is super useful. For example, I can select this two objects here, and then shift this one here, then hit CTRL + P, and set the parent to object... Did you know that you can also parent stuff directly inside the outliner over here?... Simply hold down SHIFT, then select this gallon here and drag it on top of the head, and that's it. Now these two objects are parented... if you wanna remove the parenting simply go inside here... hold down SHIFT, left click on this, move this somewhere else on to this collection here, and then you can see the info, drop to clear parent, and then the parent is gone.'
rejected_alternative: Using Ctrl+P (Set Parent To Object) from the 3D viewport for every parent/unparent action, which requires selecting both objects in the viewport rather than dragging rows in the Outliner.
reason: A lower-friction way to build and undo parent hierarchies (e.g. attaching a sub-part to a body object) directly from the Outliner while organizing collections, instead of switching back to the viewport for Ctrl+P each time.
